prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "COCA COLA CO" (ticker KO), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "KO", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The Coca-Cola Company
markets: Water, sports drinks, coffee and tea

mission.statement: to refresh the world and make a difference
mission.source: The Coca-Cola Company Form 10-K (2023), which says the company is guided by this purpose
mission.plain: Coca-Cola wants to give people tasty drinks everywhere while doing some good in the world.

about.plain: Coca-Cola owns famous drink brands like Coca-Cola, Sprite, Fanta, Powerade, Minute Maid and fairlife milk. It mostly makes the secret syrups and concentrates and sells them to bottling companies. The bottlers mix, bottle and deliver the drinks to shops, restaurants and vending machines in more than 200 countries. Coca-Cola also pays for the advertising that makes people want its drinks.
about.customers: Bottling partners, plus shops, restaurants, cinemas and vending operators that sell its drinks to people.
about.everyday: The red Coca-Cola can or bottle you can buy in almost any shop, café or fast-food restaurant in the world.

money.plain: Coca-Cola, Coke Zero Sugar, Diet Coke, Sprite and Fanta
smartwater, Dasani, Powerade, BodyArmor, Costa Coffee and Gold Peak tea
Minute Maid, Simply juices and fairlife filtered milk
company-owned bottlers that make and deliver drinks, being shrunk through refranchising (India in 2025, Africa pending)
partner drinks such as Jack Daniel's & Coca-Cola and Topo Chico Spirited

result.summary: Coca-Cola has one of the widest moats in consumer goods: the world's best-known drink brands, a global bottling system that puts its drinks within reach of almost everyone, and an asset-light concentrate model that earned a 61.6% gross margin and 28.7% operating margin on $47,941M of revenue in 2025. Rivals such as PepsiCo and Keurig Dr Pepper compete hard but have not dented its lead in sparkling drinks, though slow volume growth and health trends limit its growth.

pricingPower.evidence: In 2023 organic revenue grew 12% while unit case volume still grew 2%, and in 2025 price/mix added 4% with unit case volume flat, as the company passed inflation on to consumers; gross margin rose from 59.3% in 2020 to 61.6% in 2025.

moats.evidence: Coca-Cola is one of the world's most recognised brands and the company owns many billion-dollar brands (Coca-Cola, Sprite, Fanta, Powerade, Minute Maid, fairlife); it consistently ranks among the most valuable brands in Interbrand's annual ranking.
Consumers can switch drinks at no cost, though restaurant fountain contracts (such as McDonald's) and long-term bottler agreements create some stickiness for business customers.
Ubiquity and the bottler network reinforce each other, but there is no true user-to-user network effect.
Its scale lets it outspend rivals on marketing and gives its bottlers dense distribution routes and cooler placement in millions of outlets, which smaller brands cannot match.
In many countries the local beverage distribution market supports only one or two large bottling systems, usually Coca-Cola's and Pepsi's.
Its asset-light concentrate model is well known and copied by PepsiCo and others, so it gives no counter-positioning advantage.
Over a century of experience managing a franchised bottler system and global marketing is hard to replicate, though not unique.
The secret Coca-Cola formula and exclusive long-term agreements with independent bottlers such as Coca-Cola FEMSA, Coca-Cola HBC and Coca-Cola Europacific Partners are assets no rival can obtain.

customers.evidence: The company gained value share in total nonalcoholic ready-to-drink beverages in 2025 and again in Q2 2026, and its CSD portfolio held the leading retail volume share in 36 of 41 US metro markets tracked by Beverage Digest in 2025.

talent.evidence: Coca-Cola is a prestigious employer with deep internal succession (new CEO Henrique Braun is a 30-year company veteran), but it is not a magnet for top technical talent and it has cut staff through refranchising.

product.evidence: Coca-Cola is the best-selling soft drink in the US (about 19.2% of US carbonated soft drink volume in 2023 per Beverage Digest data), and Sprite and Diet Coke are also top-five brands.

competitors.name: PepsiCo
competitors.note: Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Aquafina, Tropicana-heritage juices and Lipton tea worldwide

competitors.name: Keurig Dr Pepper
competitors.note: Dr Pepper, Canada Dry, 7UP (US), Snapple, Core water and coffee pods in North America

competitors.note: Energy drinks; Coca-Cola owns a stake and distributes Monster through its bottlers

competitors.name: Red Bull

competitors.note: Bottled water (Nestlé Pure Life, S.Pellegrino, Perrier), coffee and ready-to-drink beverages

competitors.name: Danone
competitors.note: Bottled water (Evian, Volvic, Aqua) and plant-based and dairy drinks

competitors.note: Bottled water brands in North America (Poland Spring, Pure Life US, Primo)

competitors.name: Private-label and local soft drink makers (e.g. Ajegroup)
competitors.note: Low-priced colas and flavoured drinks in emerging markets and supermarkets

estimates.name: Private-label and local soft drink makers (e.g. Ajegroup)

marketShare.measure: sales volume share by brand (Beverage Digest data via The Wall Street Journal)

threats: Health trends, sugar taxes and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs reducing demand for sugary drinks
Flat global unit case volume in 2025, leaving growth dependent on price increases that consumers may resist
Fast-growing challengers in energy (Red Bull, Celsius), functional soda (Poppi, now PepsiCo) and Dr Pepper's US share gains
The unresolved IRS transfer-pricing tax dispute, which could cost billions
Currency swings, since most revenue comes from outside the US
Plastic packaging regulation and water-use concerns in water-stressed markets
Execution risk under a new CEO (Henrique Braun, since March 2026)

ceo.name: Henrique Braun
ceo.background: Agricultural engineer (Federal Rural University of Rio de Janeiro), MS Michigan State University, MBA Georgia State University; joined Coca-Cola in 1996 and led Greater China and South Korea, Brazil, Latin America and International Development before becoming COO in 2025 and CEO on March 31, 2026

c1.evidence: Coca-Cola leads the global non-alcoholic beverage industry, but it is a mature industry: 2025 unit case volume was flat and revenue grew 2% to $47,941M.

c2.evidence: Consumers choose it for taste, habit and the Coca-Cola brand, and the bottler system that places its drinks in millions of outlets has protected that lead for over a century.

c3.evidence: Coca-Cola is one of the most recognised names on earth and the default cola, holding the leading CSD volume share in 36 of 41 US metro markets in 2025.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'to refresh the world and make a difference' is repeated in filings, but management is mainly judged on revenue and EPS growth, and the purpose is about refreshment rather than a transformative mission.

c6.evidence: “iconic, classic, refreshing, sugary” - the impression is mostly positive and nostalgic, tempered by health concerns about sugar and criticism over plastic waste.

c7.evidence: The global non-alcoholic beverage market is very large, but it grows only in low-to-mid single digits and does not ride a fast secular trend.

c8.evidence: It keeps adding categories such as fairlife dairy, BodyArmor sports drinks, Costa coffee and alcoholic ready-to-drink partnerships, but all stay within beverages.

m1.evidence: Henrique Braun has a clear growth plan built on emerging markets and portfolio innovation, but he is a steward of a mature system rather than a futurist.

m2.evidence: Braun is a 30-year company veteran who acts as a long-term steward, but he is a professional manager, not a founder.

m4.evidence: He emphasises staying close to consumers, customers and bottling partners, but there is little public evidence of a servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: Coca-Cola's culture is strong on marketing and system management, and it launches many new flavours and brands, but it is not a technology innovator.

m6.evidence: Braun trained as an agricultural engineer and ran operations across many markets, but the role is about brands and bottling rather than technology.

m7.evidence: No controversies attach to Braun, who became CEO in March 2026, but there is little public record yet to judge his character beyond company stewardship.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Henrique Braun at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or another top university could be found.

m8b.evidence: Braun is a low-profile operator, not a celebrity CEO.

m9.evidence: As COO and head of international markets he oversaw growth that lifted revenue from $43,004M (2022) to $47,941M (2025), and his first full quarter as CEO (Q2 2026) delivered 6% organic growth, 5% volume growth and raised guidance.

m10.evidence: Coca-Cola spends heavily on marketing and is not known for frugality, though it runs productivity programmes.

c10.evidence: Its drinks are enjoyed by billions of people in more than 200 countries, but they are treats and refreshment rather than life-improving products.

p2.evidence: Making soft drinks is not technically hard; Coca-Cola's edge is its brand and distribution rather than difficult technology.

f1.evidence: Net operating revenues rose every year from $33,014M in 2020 to $38,655M, $43,004M, $45,754M, $47,061M and $47,941M in 2025.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 59.3% in 2020 to 61.6% in 2025 and operating margin from 27.3% to 28.7%, but operating margin dipped to 21.2% in 2024 because of impairments and fairlife-related charges.

f3.evidence: Total debt of $45,492M at end-2025 far exceeds cash and short-term investments of $13,872M, though it is about 3 years of underlying free cash flow and shareholders' equity is positive at $34,275M.

f4.evidence: Operating income grew from $8,997M (2020) to $13,762M (2025), but operating cash flow fell from $12,625M (2021) to $7,408M (2025), mainly because of the roughly $6B fairlife contingent payment in 2025.

v1.evidence: Many people simply prefer the taste of Coca-Cola and can find it everywhere, but in blind taste tests rivals like Pepsi are close, so 'best' is mostly a matter of preference.

v2.evidence: Coca-Cola is a well-regarded, prestigious employer, but no top placing on major best-workplace rankings could be verified.

c5.evidence: Billions of consumers and its bottling partners' hundreds of thousands of workers would miss it, but substitutes exist and health experts would not see its sugary drinks as making the world better.
